So I'm very pleased to be before you today and I'm mindful of the time. I've provided or documents. One is a short briefing note.
The second is a copy of the Edmonton by law with respect to street harassment.

The third is a copy of the September resolution from the Federation of Canadian municipalities, urging Canadian municipalities to adopt the NCCM's municipal recommendations policy recommendations on Islamophobia.
And the fourth document is actually an entire deck of the NCCM's recommendations for the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
The municipal recommendations comprise the last seven slides in that deck just to give you some context.

So this arose out of the National Summit on Islamophobia, which came about as a result of the murder of the four members of the Office of Family and Modern Ontario when a white supremacist decided to take it into his head that he should run over this family of three generations as they were waiting at a stop block.
So brief thought experiment. If you live in a ward where there's a school, a mosque, a synagogue, a church, a cafe, a restaurant, a mall, a park, a library, walking trails, biking trails.
Any place where the public can gather or come together, you will represent constituents who may face street harassment at some point in their experience in Saskatoon.
And unfortunately it's something that is becoming more prevalent across the country in many ways, and it's certainly something that's not foreign to our experience here in Saskatoon.
So what this by a lot proposes to do and what I'm asking this committee to consider is to provide a space to fill a gap in that space between criminal law sanction and doing nothing.
So for people that are accosted, harassed in the street, whether they be women, whether they be children, whether they be young or old, whether they be visible or white.

That harassment that results in the type of either misogynistic or Islamophobic or anti-Semitic or anti-first nations or anti-bipoc, any of the categories of protected rights that would be found under the Human Rights Code.

If those things happen away to cause extreme distress, harassment or intimidation, that falls short of a criminal code events, this bylaw would allow either the police or bylaw enforcement officer depending on how it's crafted to issue a ticket for such transgression.

So that people who are victimized in this way don't have to suffer in silence and without remedy, and for the small percentage of people in our community that have unexamined hatred in their heart and wish to victimize who they perceive to be vulnerable, but they understand that there'll be a sanction there'll be a consequence for their actions.
In a nutshell, that's the proposal. Edmonton has adopted this bylaw in similar by-life provided you a copy in August of last year. Calgary implemented a similar bylaw in June or July of 2022.
This bylaw or variations of it have been adopted by numerous municipalities throughout Ontario.
I think what it does is it helps to create a space where the city acknowledges the importance of respectful and encouraging and inclusive behavior between our residents or citizens.
And it provides a remedy for people who are victimized who would otherwise not have a remedy.

So that's my brief presentation. I'm happy to entertain any questions you may have and I look forward to this committee's decision to pass the motion for administration to consider this bylaw as well as the NCCM municipal recommendations.
